The word welt has two main areas of meaning — one related to the body, and one related to craftsmanship. Both are important, and you'll encounter both in everyday reading.
Meaning 1: A raised mark on the skin

This is the most common meaning you'll come across.

A welt is a raised, swollen ridge or streak that appears on the skin. It is not a cut, not a bruise, and not a blister — it is a raised bump, usually elongated (long and narrow), that forms on the surface of the skin. It is typically red or reddish-pink, tender to the touch, and stands out visibly from the surrounding skin.

How does a welt form?

A welt forms when skin is struck sharply by something, or when something irritates it. Common causes:

  • Being hit by a whip, belt, cane, rod, or strap — the sharp impact causes the skin to swell up in the shape of that blow, leaving a raised line.
  • Being struck by a branch, twig, or rope.
  • An insect sting or bite (like a bee sting or mosquito bite) — the skin puffs up into a small raised bump, which is also called a welt.
  • Allergic reactions on the skin can produce multiple welts, sometimes called hives (medically, urticaria). These are itchy, raised patches or streaks scattered across the body.

What does a welt feel like and look like?

Imagine pressing your finger firmly against your forearm and then pulling it away — that temporary raised ridge is similar in shape to a welt, except a real welt is more pronounced, persists for hours or days, and is often painful or itchy. A welt from a whip or cane looks like a swollen line across the skin, as if someone drew a thick raised stripe on it. A welt from an insect bite looks like a dome-shaped puffed-up spot.

How is a welt different from a bruise?

A bruise is discoloration under the skin — the skin stays flat but turns purple or blue because blood has leaked under the surface. A welt is different: the skin rises above its normal level. You can feel a welt by running your finger across it. A hard blow can cause both — a raised welt and an underlying bruise — but they are different things.

Example sentences:

  • "The teacher's ruler left a painful welt across the back of his hand."
  • "She came home covered in welts from the mosquitoes at the campsite."
  • "His skin broke out in angry red welts after eating shellfish."
Meaning 2: A strip of material in shoemaking or sewing

This meaning is more specialized but very commonly encountered when reading about shoes, tailoring, or clothing construction.

In shoemaking:

A welt is a narrow strip of leather (or sometimes synthetic material) that acts as the connecting bridge between different parts of a shoe.

Here is how it works: a shoe has an upper (the part that wraps around your foot) and a sole (the bottom part you walk on). The welt is stitched along the edge where they meet. It runs all the way around the perimeter of the shoe, holding everything together.

Think of the welt as the seam of a shoe — but instead of two pieces of fabric sewn directly together, a third piece (the welt) is inserted between them, giving the join extra strength and structure. This method also makes it possible to detach and replace the sole without destroying the upper — which is why shoes made this way are considered high quality and long-lasting.

You will often see the phrase "Goodyear welt" — this refers to a specific, well-regarded method of attaching the welt to the shoe by machine, named after Charles Goodyear Jr. (not the tire company). Shoes described as "Goodyear welted" are considered premium footwear.

Example sentences:

  • "These dress shoes feature a hand-stitched welt, which makes them resolable."
  • "The cobbler examined the welt carefully before deciding whether the sole could be replaced."

In sewing and tailoring:

A welt is a narrow strip of fabric used as a finished edge or border on a garment. It most famously appears in the welt pocket — a type of pocket where the opening is a horizontal slit on the outside of the garment, finished on each side with a narrow strip of fabric (the welt). This gives the pocket a clean, flat, almost invisible appearance from the outside. You'll find welt pockets on suit jackets, blazers, and trousers.

Example sentences:

  • "The tailor sewed a clean welt along the opening of the breast pocket."
  • "Welt pockets are common on formal suits because they lie flat and look sleek."

ContextWhat "welt" means
Skin / bodyA raised, swollen ridge from a blow, bite, or allergic reaction
ShoesA strip of leather connecting the upper and sole
ClothingA strip of fabric used to finish a pocket or edge

In everyday, non-specialized conversation, welt almost always refers to the raised mark on skin. When you're reading about shoes or clothing, it refers to the strip of material used in construction.

The common thread across all meanings is the idea of a strip or ridge — whether that's a raised ridge of swollen skin, a strip of leather in a shoe, or a strip of fabric on a garment. That image of a narrow, raised strip ties all the meanings together.
A quick note on the plural and usage

The plural is simply welts. It is used as a regular count noun:

  • "He had a welt on his arm."
  • "She had several welts on her back."
  • "The shoe's welts were stitched by hand."

That's everything there is to know about welt as a noun. You now have a complete picture of it.
